This ticket captures research insights from a multi-model AI code analysis experiment that directly supports Epic OSSM-12935's agentic development goals.

I ran an experiment: what happens when you unleash four different AI models on the same codebase? Turns out, when they all agree something's broken, they're almost never wrong.

## Research Overview

*Study Design*: Four AI models (GLM-5.2, Opus 4.6, Fable 5, Codex 5.3) independently analyzed the sail-operator codebase using the "ponytail methodology" to identify dead code, stdlib replacement opportunities, dependency issues, and over-engineering.

*Key Results*:
- *12 consensus findings* where all 4 models agreed (predicted 5, got 12 - math was wrong)
- *89% accuracy rate* when consensus findings matched actual GitHub issues  
- *Model specializations discovered*: GLM hates dependencies, Opus wants big refactors, Fable plays it safe, Codex prefers explicit code

## Critical Technical Findings

*Real Bugs Identified Through Consensus*:
1. *Issue #2079 (HIGH)* - Error handling that quietly drops reconcile failures (the kind that makes you sad at 2 AM)
2. *Issue #2105* - 157-line dead file with zero callers anywhere
3. *Issue #2106* - Duplicate YAML dependencies (all 4 models said "why do you have this twice?")

*Model Performance vs GitHub Issue Validation*:
- Codex 5.3: 87% accuracy (23 findings, 20 matches)
- Fable 5: 83% accuracy (18 findings, 15 matches)  
- Opus 4.6: 78% accuracy (32 findings, 25 matches)
- GLM-5.2: 72% accuracy (36 findings, 26 matches)

## Model Specialization Mapping

Each model has distinct analytical strengths that could be leveraged for specialized automation:

- *GLM-5.2*: Dependency optimization specialist - aggressive about removing unused dependencies
- *Opus 4.6*: Balanced architectural analysis - good at spotting refactoring opportunities  
- *Fable 5*: Conservative, high-confidence findings - lowest false positive rate
- *Codex 5.3*: Practical focus - flags over-abstraction, prefers explicit code

## Actionable Outcomes for Epic OSSM-12935

*Immediate Engineering Value*:
- Validated framework for multi-model code analysis as reusable AI skill
- Model routing strategy for specialized analysis tasks (send dependency questions to GLM, architecture to Opus, etc.)
- Template for reproducible AI analysis across OSSM repositories
- Consensus-based validation approach for automated code review

*Integration with Agentic Development Goals*:
1. *Complex Skills Development* - Demonstrates methodology beyond simple slash commands
2. *Team-Integrated Automation* - Provides confidence metrics for trusting AI recommendations
3. *CI Agent Enablement* - Shows how to coordinate multiple models for reliable automation
4. *CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md Enhancement* - Offers concrete multi-model coordination patterns

## The Weird Part (Research Insights)

*Consensus Effect*: Multiple models finding the same problems isn't coincidence - it's signal worth paying attention to. When 3+ models independently flag the same issue, they're almost never wrong.

*Predictability vs. Emergence*: You can predict how individual models behave mathematically, but when they work together, something unexpected happens. Consensus formation is stronger than theory suggests.

*Practical Framework*: This isn't just a one-off experiment - we built a reproducible framework that other teams can copy and modify for their codebases.

## Reproducibility Documentation

Complete methodology documented with:
- *Setup Instructions* - How to configure 4-model analysis for any repository
- *Consensus Detection Scripts* - Automated tools for finding agreement patterns
- *GitHub Issue Validation* - Process for measuring accuracy against real problems
- *Model Performance Calibration* - Techniques for understanding model strengths/weaknesses

*Documentation Location*: [Google Doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/17Hlig4OxN8mbl-HOheI3xklTdpTVY6cWPZELoS1y4Ts/edit?usp=sharing)

## Strategic Value for Epic OSSM-12935

This work gives the Epic something concrete to build on:
- Shows how to create "complex skills" that actually work (not just demos)
- Proves you can get multiple AIs to work together reliably  
- Provides a template other teams can copy and modify
- Gives confidence metrics so you know when to trust AI recommendations
- Bridges the gap between "cool experiment" and "production automation"

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Document complete methodology in OSSM knowledge base
- [ ] Create reproducible analysis template for other repositories
- [ ] Map model specializations to analysis use cases  
- [ ] Validate integration approach with existing AI configurations (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md)
- [ ] Provide recommendations for CI automation implementation
- [ ] Create follow-up tickets for implementing reusable skills

## Follow-up Work Items

Based on this research, recommend creating these additional tickets:

1. *Implement Multi-Model Analysis Skill* - Convert research methodology into reusable AI skill for OSSM repositories
2. *Model Specialization Framework* - Create routing logic to send different types of analysis to specialized models  
3. *Consensus-Based Code Review Automation* - CI integration that triggers on high-confidence consensus findings
4. *Critical Issue Remediation* - Address the specific consensus findings (#2079 error handling, #2105 dead code)

## Links and References

- *Epic*: OSSM-12935 - OSSM Agentic Software Development Lifecycle
- *Analysis Documentation*: [Google Doc Presentation](https://docs.google.com/document/d/17Hlig4OxN8mbl-HOheI3xklTdpTVY6cWPZELoS1y4Ts/edit?usp=sharing)
- *GitHub Issues Validated*: 
  - [#2079](https://github.com/istio-ecosystem/sail-operator/issues/2079) - Error handling that silently drops failures (HIGH)
  - [#2105](https://github.com/istio-ecosystem/sail-operator/issues/2105) - ZTunnel dead API fields  
  - [#2106](https://github.com/istio-ecosystem/sail-operator/issues/2106) - Duplicate YAML dependencies

OSSM 2.6 docs are currently published in OCP documentation versions that 2,6 is not supported in. Need to remove them. Instructions are in [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fLMpK4bqthtFlCwA36yeo2cI-pExFpX76VMnSi_In6Q/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.kogyc4swtaab|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fLMpK4bqthtFlCwA36yeo2cI-pExFpX76VMnSi_In6Q/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.kogyc4swtaab|smart-link] 



Unpublish the splash page for the published version to remove:

* Open the [+Splash Page Manager+|https://pantheon.cee.redhat.com/#/splash-pages] from Pantheon.
* Select the version for OpenShift Container Platform that you want to remove.
* Follow the steps documented in the Pantheon user guide to [+unpublish a splash page+|https://pantheon.cee.redhat.com/help/user-guide/#unpublishing_a_splash_page].



Note that unpublishing the splash page does not remove the books for this version that have been published. If the release is coming soon, then just unpublishing the splash page might be sufficient. 



If the release is completely in error, or is being delayed a significant amount of time, then you might need to consider also removing the published books so that they can’t be accessed by their URLs anymore. To do that, follow the steps in the Pantheon user guide for [+deleting titles+|https://pantheon.cee.redhat.com/help/user-guide/#workflow-deleting]*.*

The {{external-puller}} SA is used to pull Konflux images in Jenkins. The Jenkins CSB declaration must be updated accordingly:
* GitLab MR: https://gitlab.cee.redhat.com/istio/servicemesh-qe/jenkins-csb-declaration/-/merge_requests/885

h2. Migration Steps

h1. Identify which predefined SA name ({{konflux-bot-0}}, {{konflux-bot-1}}, or {{konflux-bot-2}}) to assign to each current SA
h1. Update the Jenkins CSB declaration to reference the new SA name instead of {{external-puller}} (coordinate with servicemesh-qe)
h1. Migrate any secrets (e.g. {{external-puller-token}}) to the new predefined SA
h1. Update the GitOps application {{service-mesh-tenant-stone-prod-p02}} if it references the {{nid-team}} SA
h1. Verify image pulls in Jenkins continue to work with the new SA
h1. Remove/decommission the old custom SAs before the July 30th deadline

h4. *Bring full implementation to 3.5; enable Network Policies by default for OCP 5 via 3.4 z-stream*

This strategy moves the universal default enablement to version 3.5. For the 3.4.x z-stream, the system would detect the OCP version at runtime, enabling NPs by default only for OCP 5 clusters while maintaining the opt-in model for OCP 4.

 

----

 

||*Pros*||*Cons*||
|* Directly addresses the platform requiring the change.|* Requires OCP version detection|
|* Avoids breaking changes for OCP 4 users.|* Introduces a behavioral shift within a z-stream (though restricted to OCP 5).|
|* Satisfies the "NPs required for OCP 5.0" mandate.|* Version detection logic requires maintenance.|
|* Can be framed as a "platform compatibility" update.|* Increases complexity in the defaults pipeline with conditional logic.|

 

----

 

 

Implementation:

# *OCP Version Detection*: Create logic to query the `[+config.openshift.io/v1`+|http://config.openshift.io/v1%60] ClusterVersion API and parse `.status.desired.version`. Follow the pattern of `DetectPlatform()` in `pkg/config/platform.go`.
# *Configuration Storage*: Integrate the detected OCP version into `ReconcilerConfig` for use during values calculation.
# *Conditional Defaults*: Implement branching in `ApplyVendorDefaults` based on the OCP major version, or establish a dedicated OCP 5 profile/overlay.
# *Foundational Tasks*: Complete prerequisite work including API types and ztunnel vendor defaults.

This will live in midstream, not in upstream sail-operator.

items.toString:
In an Istio ambient mesh multi-primary setup on different networks (east/west clusters connected via east-west gateways with double-HBONE), enrolling the *source* cluster's namespace in a waypoint causes cross-cluster traffic to fail with RBAC denial on the destination side.

* *East cluster*: runs {{sleep}} pod in {{sample}} namespace
* *West cluster*: runs {{helloworld}} pod in {{sample}} namespace
* *Works*: east {{sample}} namespace has no waypoint
* *Broken*: east {{sample}} namespace enrolled in waypoint

EW gateway sees {{x-istio-source: waypoint}} → skips west waypoint → routes directly to helloworld → AuthorizationPolicy enforced at L4 → can't evaluate HTTP headers → denied.

*Root Cause*

The code assumes that if traffic has already passed through *any* waypoint, all L7 policies have been applied, and unconditionally skips the destination waypoint. This assumption is wrong — source and destination waypoints serve different roles. The source waypoint enforces policies on the outgoing side; the destination waypoint enforces policies for the destination service. Skipping the destination waypoint leaves its L7 policies unenforced.

items.fromString:
*Motivation and Background*

A typical OSSM customer upgrades Istio around once per year. In this case, they would like to jump from a year old version to the most recent version - which may involve jumping up to 4 Istio releases. This is especially true of recent customers who have updated form 2.6 to 3.0 and will want to jump to 3.4. This is also a requirement for OCP 5.2’s extended support for service mesh.

Skipping Istio versions should be supported in Istio and the sail-operator with the revision based (canary-style) upgrade procedure, though may come with more risks due to the delta in Envoy and Istiod versions, as well as other factors.

*Outcome*

A documented (and tested) procedure for upgrading OpenShift Service Mesh across up to 4 Istio releases with only one workload restart required. This should include notes on potential risks - in particular, anything that might cause application interruptions or downtime.
items.toString:
*Motivation and Background*

OSSM customers running sidecar mode typically upgrade once per year. With Istio's quarterly release cadence, that means jumping 3–4 minor versions. Today this requires sequential hop-by-hop upgrades, each needing its own operator update and a full workload restart cycle. This is operationally expensive, especially in environments with large numbers of namespaces and strict change management windows.

This epic delivers a supported path for upgrading sidecar mode across **up to 4 Istio minor versions** in a single administrative action: one `Istio` CR update, one workload rolling restart.

Because istiod is the shared control plane for both data plane modes, the control plane skip-level work is scoped to this epic — it runs first and is the foundation for everything in OSSM-14857. Any istiod changes specific to ambient mode (e.g. ztunnel xDS compatibility) are tracked in OSSM-14857, not here.

*How Sidecar Skip-Level Might Work*

Sidecar mode uses Istio's **revision-based canary upgrade**:

# The sail-operator creates a new `IstioRevision` targeting the new Istio version.

# A new istiod deployment starts alongside the existing one.

# Workload namespaces are relabeled (`[istio.io/rev=|http://istio.io/rev=]<new-revision>`).

# Application pods are restarted, picking up the new sidecar version and connecting to the new istiod.

# The old revision is removed once all workloads have migrated.

This mechanism is well-tested for N-1 hops. For skip-level, the question is: **can step 4 safely jump more than one minor version?** The answer depends on whether the new istiod can serve xDS to the old sidecar during the transition window (step 2–4), and whether the new sidecar can function correctly without any intermediate-version configuration state.

Two approaches exist (see OCPSTRAT-3410 Technical Question #1):

* **Approach A (operator-orchestrated hops):** The sail-operator creates intermediate revisions internally, stepping through each minor version. The administrator sees a single CR update; the operator handles the sequence. Old sidecar proxies only ever need to talk to an istiod that is one minor version ahead.

* **Approach B (extended xDS compatibility):** Upstream Istio extends backward compatibility so a 1.34 istiod can serve 1.30 sidecars. The operator creates a single target revision and workloads jump directly. Simpler operator, but requires upstream changes.

Either way, the administrator updates the `Istio` CR once and restarts pods once.

*Outcome*

A documented (and tested) procedure for upgrading OpenShift Service Mesh across up to 4 Istio releases with only one workload restart required. This should include notes on potential risks - in particular, anything that might cause application interruptions or downtime.

Here is a comprehensive and structured Jira description tailored for Phase 3 of your AI Chatbot project, focusing on stability, context retention, and user experience.

h3. *Title / Summary*

[TP] Enhance AI Chatbot: Context Awareness & UX Improvements (Phase 3)

h3. *Background / Context*

Following the successful deployment of the chatbot MVP in earlier phases, user feedback and monitoring have highlighted areas requiring stabilization and refinement. Currently, the chatbot occasionally loses conversational context during multi-turn interactions and suffers from edge-case crashes (e.g., API timeouts) that result in a poor user experience. Phase 3 focuses on making the chatbot more robust, intelligent, and user-friendly by upgrading state management and hardening error handling.

h3. *Problem Statement*

* *Context Drops:* The bot treats sequential questions as isolated queries, forcing users to repeat themselves.
* *Brittle Error Handling:* When the LLM provider times out or fails, the UI freezes or displays a generic, unhelpful error message.
* *UX Friction:* Lack of visual feedback (e.g., typing indicators, clear formatting) makes the bot feel unresponsive and less engaging.

h3. *Key Deliverables*

# *Context Awareness (Backend & Logic)*

* Implement a robust state management system to retain user context across a single session.
* Configure a rolling context window to accurately pass the last 5-10 conversation turns to the LLM.
* Add payload truncation logic to ensure the enriched context does not exceed token limits or cause API rejections.

# *Stability & Error Handling (Full Stack)*

* Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for transient LLM API failures.
* Create graceful fallback responses when the service is definitively unavailable (e.g., "I'm having trouble connecting right now, please try again in a moment").
* Add frontend timeout handlers to prevent the UI from hanging indefinitely.

# *UX Improvements (Frontend)*

* Add a smooth "typing..." indicator (or skeleton loader) while waiting for the LLM response.
* Improve Markdown rendering in the chat window to better support code blocks, bold text, and lists.
* Implement a "Clear Conversation" button so users can manually reset the context state when switching topics.

h3. *Acceptance Criteria*

* The chatbot successfully remembers constraints or subjects mentioned in previous prompts during a single session.
* The chatbot gracefully handles simulated API timeouts, displaying a user-friendly error message within 15 seconds instead of freezing.
* The frontend correctly displays a visual loading state immediately after the user submits a message.
* The frontend successfully parses and renders Markdown elements (bolding, lists, and code blocks) returned by the LLM.
* Clicking the "Clear Conversation" button successfully purges the backend session state and resets the UI.
* All new logic is covered by unit tests, ensuring context assembly and error fallbacks function as expected.

items.toString:
With the upcoming merge of [kubernetes-mcp-server/pull/920|https://github.com/containers/kubernetes-mcp-server/pull/920], the foundational Model Context Protocol (MCP) server now supports *MCP Apps* (spec version 2026-01-26). This extension allows LLM tools to return rich, interactive UI components rendered within sandboxed iframes by MCP hosts (like VS Code Copilot, Claude, and Goose).

We need to integrate this upstream capability into our {{kiali-ossm}} MCP implementation. This will allow us to bring Kiali's powerful visualization capabilities—such as topology graphs, metrics dashboards, and Istio configuration forms—directly into the user's AI chat interfaces.

h3. *Background & Upstream Implementation Details*

The upstream PR introduces a lightweight, zero-overhead (when disabled) approach to rendering UIs that we must align with:

* *Opt-in Design:* Controlled via an {{apps_enabled}} configuration or {{--apps}} CLI flag.
* *Tech Stack:* Uses Preact + HTM with Signals-core (~19 KB), avoiding heavy frameworks like Alpine.js.
* *No Build Step:* Libraries are inlined in HTML, meaning no Node.js/npm dependencies are required to build the server.
* *Airgap Ready:* JavaScript dependencies are vendored and committed to the repository.
* *Protocol:* Implements the UI extension protocol directly via host-fetched HTML resources and bidirectional {{postMessage}} JSON-RPC communication.

h3. *Goals for Kiali Integration*

By adopting this, Kiali MCP can transition from returning static text/JSON summaries to providing embedded interactive experiences.

*Potential Kiali UI Widgets (Candidates for Subtasks)*

|*Feature Area*|*Interactive MCP App Concept*|
|*Topology*|Visual mini-graph of workloads, routing, and traffic health.|
|*Metrics*|Interactive charts for inbound/outbound traffic, latency, and error rates.|
|*Validations*|Sortable and filterable tables highlighting Istio config errors/warnings.|
|*Actions*|Forms to quickly generate or edit AuthorizationPolicies or PeerAuthentications.|

----

* Add EOL notice in release notes

* Archive OSSM 2.6-specific documentation

This story is about adding e2e integration tests for verifying metrics integration in Sail Operator.

Acceptance Criteria:
1. Add e2e environment setup 
- Upstream Sail Operator need e2e environment setup for KinD + Prometheus .   This can be done by the existing KinD e2e setup with the upstream Istio Prometheus sample, e.g. {{kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/istio/istio/master/samples/addons/prometheus.yaml}}  The difference is that all scraping job configurations are included in the upstream Istio Prometheus.yaml . The Sail Operator metric integration will use new controller to call {{ServiceMonitor}} and {{PodMonitor}} to update those scraping jobs.
- Midstream Sail Operator need e2e environment setup for OpenShift + default Prometheus stack or OpenShift + COO monitoring stack.  This can be done by adding additional CI jobs scripts in:
[https://github.com/openshift/release/tree/main/ci-operator/step-registry/servicemesh/sail-operator|https://github.com/openshift/release/tree/main/ci-operator/step-registry/servicemesh/sail-operator|smart-link] 
The size of adding this midstream e2e setup is XXL

2. Implement e2e Sail Operator tests for verifying new controller expected use cases.
